nodes.description: Reduced hepatic glucose output during fasting produces hypoglycaemia that is usually mild, because gluconeogenesis compensates. Intact fatty-acid oxidation shifts metabolism toward lipid, so ketone bodies rise. Ketosis is therefore a positive, expected finding here and can occur even when hypoglycaemia is slight - the discriminating feature against GSD I.

nodes.description: Poor growth is a presenting feature alongside hepatomegaly, and short stature with delayed puberty is a recognised complication of suboptimal metabolic control.

evidence.snippet: More common complications in the setting of suboptimal metabolic control include short stature, delayed puberty, osteopenia, and osteoporosis.

nodes.description: This is the node that contradicts the disease's reputation. Across 37 biopsies in the largest systematic review, liver fibrosis was present in 32.4% and early cirrhosis in 10.8%; a Chinese series independently found regenerative nodules in four of ten patients. Note the ascertainment caveat: these are proportions of BIOPSIED patients, not of all patients, and biopsy is not performed at random. The honest summary is that the typical course is mild and diet-responsive while fibrosis is common in those biopsied and cirrhosis is uncommon but real.

evidence.snippet: Our review demonstrates that GSD VI is a disorder with broad clinical heterogeneity and a small number of patients with a severe phenotype and liver cirrhosis.

evidence.reference_title: Glycogen storage disease type VI can progress to cirrhosis: ten Chinese patients with GSD VI and a literature review.
evidence.snippet: For the first time, we found that four Chinese patients showed cirrhosis in liver biopsy characterized by the formation of regenerative nodules.
Hepatic fibrosis commonly develops in GSD VI, but cirrhosis and hypertrophic cardiomyopathy are rare.

nodes.description: Hepatocytes accumulate structurally normal glycogen - diastase-sensitive and PAS-positive, not the abnormal polyglucosan of GSD IV. Glycogen content was increased in 89.2% of biopsies in the largest series, and in the Pygl-null mouse accumulation is progressive with age, which is the mechanistic link to the late hepatic complications.

evidence.snippet: Liver biopsies (n = 37) showed an increased glycogen content in 89.2%, liver fibrosis in 32.4% and early liver cirrhosis in 10.8% of cases, respectively.

nodes.description: Biallelic PYGL loss of function removes the liver isoform of glycogen phosphorylase, the rate-limiting enzyme of glycogenolysis, which cleaves the alpha-1,4 bonds of glycogen to release glucose-1-phosphate. The enzyme is the substrate enzyme of the hepatic phosphorylase system; its activating kinase, phosphorylase kinase, is a distinct protein whose deficiency causes the separate disease GSD IX.

evidence.reference_title: Diagnosis and management of glycogen storage diseases type VI and IX: a clinical practice resource of the American College of Medical Genetics and Genomics (ACMG).
evidence.snippet: GSD VI is caused by deficient activity of hepatic glycogen phosphorylase, an enzyme encoded by the PYGL gene.

genetic_context.description: Biallelic germline loss-of-function alleles. Residual enzyme activity is variable, which is one candidate explanation for the wide clinical range, though no clear genotype-phenotype correlation has been established.

nodes.description: The mechanistic route from glycogen overload to the hepatic complications runs through activation of hepatic stellate cells. In aged Pygl-null mice the number of alpha-SMA-positive activated stellate cells is increased, with periportal and perisinusoidal collagen deposition, portal inflammatory infiltrates, raised Ccl5 and Mcp-1, and elevated transaminases. This is the conserved mesenchymal-activation step of the fibrotic response, substituting the hepatic stellate cell as the organ-specific effector.

evidence.snippet: The main presenting symptoms were hepatomegaly and poor growth, while the most common laboratory findings at initial presentation comprised elevated activity of liver transaminases, hypertriglyceridemia, fasting hypoglycemia and postprandial hyperlactatemia.

nodes.description: This node is defined as much by what remains intact as by what fails. Glycogen breakdown is blocked, but glycogen synthesis, gluconeogenesis and fatty-acid oxidation are all preserved. That combination produces the two signatures of the disease: glycogen accumulates because synthesis continues unopposed, and fasting hypoglycaemia is comparatively mild and ketotic because gluconeogenesis can be upregulated and ketogenesis is available. The negative content of this node is the whole contrast with GSD I, where glucose-6-phosphatase failure blocks gluconeogenesis too and the hypoglycaemia is severe and non-ketotic.

nodes.description: A Pygl-deficient mouse that reproduces both arms of the human disease - the metabolic signature in young animals and the hepatic complications in old ones - and supplies the stellate-cell mechanism linking them.

Management is dietary rather than pharmacological. Frequent feeds with uncooked cornstarch provide slow-release glucose that substitutes for the absent glycogenolytic output overnight and between meals; added dietary protein supplies gluconeogenic substrate, which works here precisely because gluconeogenesis is intact. Because the intervention replaces the missing hepatic glucose output rather than correcting the enzyme, it is curated as acting on the fasting-intolerance node, not on the enzymatic lesion.
nodes.id: Uncooked Cornstarch and High-Protein Dietary Therapy

evidence.snippet: Treatment with a high-protein, low-carbohydrate diet and cornstarch improves growth and stamina and ameliorates biochemical abnormalities including hypoglycemia and ketosis.
